request.description: Train a fresh PPO candidate with the currently recorded baseline recipe for the full 120,000-step startup allocation.
request.rationale: The decisive initial distinction is whether a learned torque policy under the existing implementation can acquire and sustain the required uninterrupted hold, versus whether its apparent limitations concentrate in the official inner-radius region omitted from baseline exposure. There is no candidate or behavior evidence yet. This training run creates the first reproducible artifact and a learning trajectory; after completion, training proxies will nominate (not establish) which saved checkpoint to evaluate on the official development distribution with reach/hold and target-stratified diagnostics. The recipe's 14–20 cm training range is a known limitation, so this run is a baseline capability probe, not evidence that the coverage gap causes any later failure. A checkpoint with broadly successful reach and hold would reduce the urgency of altering control; failures after timely reach with interrupted/short holds would prioritize stabilization, while failures concentrated at 6–14 cm would motivate a controlled coverage investigation. The result is worthwhile now because no prior artifact exists to measure or compare.

request.description: Compare the first late-plateau checkpoint with the terminal checkpoint on the fixed task-reference panel and a paired 200-episode official-range research panel, retaining episode diagnostics.
request.rationale: T1's training proxy reaches 0.97 at 110,592 steps and remains 0.96–0.97 through 120,832, but those proxies are generated under the baseline 14–20 cm training sampler and cannot establish official-distribution success. The two checkpoints are complete artifacts from the same fresh run and both are supported by the observed plateau; comparing them on the same development evidence tests whether the additional training after the first plateau improves the actual task rather than assuming the terminal artifact is best. The protected task-reference panel assesses saved-policy performance under the protected development execution path. The paired research panel uses official target sampling and preserves per-episode first-reach, maximum hold, interruptions, radius and angle so that failures can be separated into reach/hold and target-region patterns. If the later checkpoint materially improves protected success without changing the relevant failure profile, it is the stronger candidate artifact; similar results imply no demonstrated benefit from the additional training. Timely reach followed by interrupted/short holds would prioritize stabilization; failures concentrated at 6–14 cm would motivate a controlled coverage test, but this comparison cannot establish coverage as the cause because training exposure and all other recipe factors are common to both checkpoints. Disagreement between protected and research outcomes would limit mechanism claims and call for investigating execution-semantics differences. These outcomes discriminate whether to continue this baseline recipe, investigate hold control, or test official-range coverage, directly toward the 98% complete-episode goal.

request.reason: Among the only two candidates measured, T1:checkpoint-110592 has the stronger completed-episode evidence: 90.5% (181/200) on the fixed task-reference panel versus 85.5% (171/200) for T1:checkpoint-120832, and 86% versus 84% on the paired official-range research panel. The paired research outcomes are modest (four discordant episodes, all won by this candidate), so this is a provisional best-known role, not proof of broad superiority or achievement of the 98% goal. It is the more defensible artifact for continuity while a causal training-exposure comparison is investigated.

request.candidates_and_roles: Best-known: T1:checkpoint-110592, explicitly assigned by E1 based on M1 (90.5% task-reference; 86% paired research) versus T1:checkpoint-120832 (85.5%; 84%). No working candidate. T1:checkpoint-120832 is an available measured comparison artifact, not the selected best-known. Neither is near the 98% objective or officially assessed. T1 archived 24 checkpoints; only the two late-plateau checkpoints were development-measured, selected because training proxies had plateaued at 0.97 and the purpose was to test whether additional training beyond the first plateau helped. No inference is made about unmeasured checkpoints.
request.cumulative_resource_use: One fresh training operation (T1): 120,000 requested, 120,832 completed due to rollout rounding; seed 42; 24 checkpoints archived. One measurement operation (M1): two task-reference evaluations and two paired 200-episode research evaluations across the two selected checkpoints. One model-role event (E1) assigning best-known. No source files changed, no extra training runs, and no official assessment. Current session completed operations: T1, M1, E1.
request.current_goal_gap: T1's baseline PPO training proxy reached 0.97 success on its 14–20 cm training range, but this does not transfer to official performance. On the protected task-reference panel the better measured checkpoint, T1:checkpoint-110592, succeeded on 181/200 episodes (90.5%); on a separate paired official-range research panel it succeeded on 172/200 (86%). This is 15 fewer successes than the 196/200 final-panel threshold on the task-reference panel and 24 failures in the research panel. No final official assessment has occurred.
request.current_synthesis: Observed: No candidate or previous operation existed at startup. T1 was a fresh PPO run under unchanged baseline sources, seed 42, 120,000 requested steps; it completed 120,832 steps after rollout rounding and archived 24 checkpoints. The training success proxy rose from 0 to 0.97 by 110,592 steps and remained 0.96–0.97 through 120,832 on the baseline 14–20 cm sampler. The run therefore establishes an executable baseline recipe and a plateau, not development success under the official distribution. M1 compared the first plateau checkpoint (110,592) with the terminal checkpoint (120,832), both from the same run and recipe. T1:checkpoint-110592 scored 90.5% (181/200) on the fixed task-reference panel and 86% (172/200) on the paired 200-episode official-range research panel. T1:checkpoint-120832 scored 85.5% (171/200) and 84% (168/200), respectively. On the paired research panel there were four discordant episodes, all won by checkpoint-110592; this is a modest artifact-level advantage, not strong evidence of a generally superior method or of a cause. The two panel types used different seeds, so their score differences do not isolate evaluator semantics. The later checkpoint had no measured task advantage despite similar training proxies; it is not privileged because it is terminal. The task-reference failure rows for both checkpoints are overwhelmingly at radii below about 11.5 cm, with a few failures at larger radii. In the research diagnostics, checkpoint-110592 had 28 failures: 21 never entered tolerance at a sampled control step, all on targets at 6.1–11.4 cm; seven reached tolerance but never completed a 100-step uninterrupted hold. Checkpoint-120832 had 32 failures: 23 never entered tolerance, also all at 6.1–11.4 cm, and nine reached tolerance but did not complete the hold. Many other inner-radius targets succeeded, and the no-reach episodes cluster in particular target-angle sectors; thus radial training coverage is a consequential hypothesis, not an established cause. Successful/reaching episodes typically first entered tolerance within roughly 5–20 control steps, so the reset singularity is real but the current evidence does not identify slow escape as the dominant failure for reached targets. The observations preserve only control-step diagnostics, not joint/torque trajectories or within-step excursions. Interpretations: The source model's kinematic feasibility conclusion remains unrevised; measured failures concern policy behavior, not proof of geometric impossibility. The training sampler omits 6–14 cm, which is 4/7 (about 57%) of official radial probability under the uniform-radius sampler and requires more folded configurations. Concentrated inner-radius failures support prioritizing a controlled coverage test. Their angular concentration, repeated no-reach patterns across the paired checkpoints, and several hold failures leave plausible alternatives: target-sector/IK-branch selection, difficulty leaving the singular reset for those configurations, and stabilization after first reach. The comparison changed checkpoint time within one training trajectory, not training distribution, and cannot establish any of those mechanisms. Dynamic path costs, compiled inertias/contact response, and within-control-step hold semantics remain unmeasured; they should change the immediate direction only if coverage-focused work fails or later traces implicate them. A research-evaluation success is measured at the accessible control-step cadence; it does not resolve hidden substep checks or certify the official final panel.
request.decision_frontier: The unresolved distinction is whether the main actionable development gap comes from the known radial exposure mismatch (especially 6–11.5 cm targets) or instead from angle/IK-branch-dependent acquisition from the singular reset and/or hold stabilization. M1's repeated no-reach failures below about 11.5 cm support the exposure hypothesis, but inner-radius successes, angular clustering, and post-reach hold failures prevent causal attribution. A useful discriminator is a fresh full-budget run holding PPO architecture, parameters, source except the training-radius lower bound, seed and evaluation protocol fixed, changing exposure from 14–20 cm to the official 6–20 cm; measure both candidates on the same held-out task-reference and research panels and inspect success, first reach, maximum hold, interruptions and target radius/angle. Improvement concentrated among inner-radius targets would support coverage as a contributor; no improvement or persistent angle-specific no-reach failures would redirect toward reset/branch/trajectory mechanisms; timely reaches followed by interrupted holds would prioritize stabilization. Because this is one recipe and one seed, either result is limited to that implementation and would not prove or disprove broader coverage methods. If coverage does not change the decision, branch-conditioned joint/endpoint trajectories and torque response are the next physical discriminator; compiled dynamics and within-step hold details remain open but are not required to prioritize the first comparison.
request.human_goal_connection: The sole objective is at least 98% complete-episode success under the official 6–20 cm, full-angle target distribution, where success requires the uninterrupted 100-step/2-second hold. This startup work established a first learned baseline, measured two plausible checkpoints on development evidence, and chose an evidence-backed best-known artifact; both measured artifacts remain materially below the goal.
request.next_direction_or_closure: Startup evidence is sufficient to checkpoint and enter goal review, not to request official assessment. The proposed next direction is a bounded, seed-matched test of the official-radius training-coverage hypothesis, subject to goal review's independent choice. The prospective comparison changes only the training-radius lower bound and evaluates complete episodes plus target-stratified reach/hold diagnostics; if it improves inner-radius success, coverage becomes a supported contributor worth developing, while persistent angular/branch or hold failures redirect the next bounded work. A null/limited result would be unresolved for the broader method, not proof that coverage cannot help. Do not infer causation from M1's checkpoint comparison.
request.next_question: Does changing only the baseline training-radius range from 14–20 cm to the official 6–20 cm improve complete-episode success, particularly for inner-radius targets, or do the observed angle-specific no-reach and post-reach hold failures persist and make reset/IK-branch control or stabilization the more consequential next direction?

request.closure_condition: Complete one fresh PPO run with the existing 120,000-step allocation and seed 42, unchanged baseline algorithm, parameters, reward, observation, runtime and task mechanics, changing only the training sampler's lower radius from 14 cm to 6 cm. Select a development-measured checkpoint using its training trajectory in that changed exposure context, not terminal status alone. Evaluate it on the same fixed task-reference panel and the same 200-episode research panel used for T1:checkpoint-110592, with paired outcomes and target-stratified success, first-reach step, maximum held steps and hold interruptions. Close with the measured candidate comparison and the behavioral pattern: inner-radius gains support coverage as a contributor; little/no gain with persistent angle-specific no-reach failures redirects toward reset/branch acquisition; timely reaches followed by failed holds redirects toward stabilization. One seed supports only this recipe-specific conclusion; a null result does not disprove broader coverage methods.
request.goal_connection: The human objective is at least 196 successes on the fixed 200-episode official panel. T1:checkpoint-110592, the strongest measured artifact, scored 181/200 (90.5%) on the separate fixed task-reference panel and 172/200 (86%) on the paired official-range research panel. Baseline training excludes 6–14 cm, about 57% of official uniform-radius probability; in M1, 21/28 and 23/32 research-panel failures never reached tolerance, all at 6.1–11.4 cm, while 7 and 9 other failures did reach but did not complete the hold. Testing whether coverage changes complete-episode outcomes therefore directly addresses the current goal gap while preserving competing acquisition and stabilization explanations.
request.question: Does a fresh, full-budget PPO run that changes only the baseline training-radius lower bound from 14 cm to 6 cm improve complete-episode success on the official distribution, especially for inner-radius targets, or do angle-specific no-reach and post-reach hold failures persist enough to redirect development toward reset/IK-branch control or stabilization?
request.rationale: Official assessment is terminal and the strongest measured candidate is materially below goal on both development panels, so its expected chance of meeting 196/200 is not compelling enough to spend the only assessment now. Further training on the unchanged recipe is also weakly supported: T1's success proxy rose to 0.94–0.96 by about 80k, fluctuated at 0.94–0.97 thereafter, and M1 found the terminal checkpoint 10/200 below the earlier plateau checkpoint on task-reference and 4/200 worse on the paired research panel. The proposed experiment is a genuinely untested training exposure, not a relabeling of T1: the inspected training environment has a single 14–20 cm sampler constant, T1 used the unchanged source commit and baseline PPO settings, and the requested comparison changes that range to 6–20 cm while holding seed and remaining recipe fixed. Its full training cost is substantial, but the known 57% radial omission and repeated inner-radius no-reach failures make it more likely to improve the route to the goal than another baseline checkpoint measurement. M1 also supplies counterevidence: many inner-radius targets succeeded, failures clustered by angle, and 7–9 failures per candidate were post-reach hold failures, so coverage is a hypothesis rather than an established cause. Research diagnostics sample control steps and cannot establish hidden within-step hold behavior or certify the official panel; this experiment can direct development but cannot substitute for final assessment.
